meta.titre: Simulation and Modelling: what-if tests on a computer model
meta.sous_theme: Models, simulations, advantages, disadvantages and what-if analysis

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Computer Science past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A trader in Bafoussam wonders what will happen to her profit if she raises the price of a product. She could try it in her shop and risk losing customers, or she could try it first on a spreadsheet. Pilots, engineers and weather offices make the same choice every day: they test on a computer before they act in real life. The GCE asks you to define simulation and to give its advantages and disadvantages with a concrete example.

items: A spreadsheet recalculates its formulas when a value in a cell is changed.
Profit equals total income minus total costs.
A variable is a quantity that can take different values.

sections.titre: Simulation and modelling: testing ideas on a computer
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Model and simulation

A **model** is a representation of a real system made of variables, rules and formulas, for example a spreadsheet that calculates profit. A **computer simulation** is the use of a model on a computer to imitate how a real system behaves, so that the user can change the inputs and study the results without using the real thing. Examples: flight simulators for pilots, testing designs of buildings or bridges, weather forecasting, and training for dangerous jobs.

### Steps in a simulation

1. Identify the real system and the questions to answer.
2. Build the model with its variables and rules.
3. Enter data and run the model.
4. Compare the results with real results and correct the model if they disagree.
5. Change values and repeat to study different cases.

### Advantages

| Advantage | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Safe | Dangerous situations such as engine failure in flight can be practised without risk |
| Cheaper | No need to build a real bridge or crash a real car to test an idea |
| Saves time | Slow events can be speeded up and fast ones slowed down |
| Repeatable | The same test can be run again and again with different values |
| Possible | It can test cases that cannot be done in real life |

For a bridge, engineers can test heavy loads and strong winds on the model before building, so weak points are found early, without risk or large cost.

### Disadvantages

- The results are only as good as the model and the data: wrong rules or wrong data give wrong results.
- Building a good model needs skill, time and money.
- A simulation cannot fully copy real life, so real tests are still needed at the end.

### What-if analysis

Changing an input in a spreadsheet and watching the formulas recalculate the results is a simple simulation called **what-if analysis**. It helps people such as shop owners to plan before they act.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to describe one advantage in a given situation
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write the advantage, then the reason, then link it to the situation. Example: it is safer, because a trainee pilot can practise an emergency on the computer where a mistake cannot crash an aircraft. A bare word such as cheaper earns no mark.
Name the limit and explain it. Example: the simulation can give wrong results because the model may leave out something that matters in real life, or the data entered may be wrong.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes someone trying different values to see the results
variantes.contenu_markdown: Trying different values in the cells of a model to see their effect on the result is **what-if analysis**, a form of simulation. The formulas stay the same and only the input values change.

sections.enonce_markdown: Mr Tabi sells bags of rice in Bafoussam. His model has these inputs: bags sold 200, selling price 500 FCFA per bag, cost 350 FCFA per bag and fixed costs 15,000 FCFA. The profit formula is `=B1*(B2-B3)-B4`, where B1 is bags sold, B2 is the price, B3 is the cost and B4 is the fixed costs. (a) Calculate the profit. (b) What is the profit if the price rises to 550 FCFA? (c) What is the profit if the price is 550 FCFA but sales fall to 150 bags? (d) What can he conclude, and what is this technique called?

etapes.action: Write the profit rule in words.
etapes.justification: The formula gives income minus costs: bags sold times profit per bag, minus fixed costs.
Replace the cells by their values.
Only B2 changes; the other inputs stay the same.
A higher price may reduce the number of customers, so B1 also changes.
Compare the three cases with the base case.
etapes.resultat_markdown: A price rise helps only if sales do not fall too far.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Profit is 15,000 FCFA at first, 25,000 FCFA if the price rises with no loss of customers, and 15,000 FCFA if sales fall to 150 bags, the same as at the start. Mr Tabi learns this without risking his shop. The technique is what-if analysis, a simple computer simulation.

items.erreur_markdown: A simulation always gives exact, real results.
items.pourquoi_faux: The results depend on the model and the data, so they may be wrong if either is wrong.
items.correction_markdown: A simulation gives **predictions** that are only as accurate as the model.

items.erreur_markdown: A model and a simulation are the same thing.
items.pourquoi_faux: The model is the representation. The simulation is the act of running the model with chosen values.
items.correction_markdown: **Model**: the representation. **Simulation**: using it to imitate the system.

items.erreur_markdown: Simulation removes the need for any real testing.
items.pourquoi_faux: The model may miss something, so final real tests are still necessary.
items.correction_markdown: Simulation **reduces** real testing but does not replace it completely.

items.erreur_markdown: One advantage is that it is cheaper. (No further explanation.)
items.pourquoi_faux: A bare word does not show understanding and rarely gets the mark.
items.correction_markdown: Add the reason and the situation: no real prototype has to be built, so money is saved.

items.erreur_markdown: Simulations are used only for dangerous activities.
items.pourquoi_faux: They are also used when an activity is too slow, too costly or impossible to repeat in real life.
items.correction_markdown: Examples: weather forecasting, business planning and **spreadsheet what-if** tests.

items.enonce_markdown: Define a computer simulation and give two examples of its use.
items.solution_markdown:
A computer simulation is the use of a computer model to imitate how a real system behaves, so that it can be studied without using the real system.

Examples: **flight simulators** for training pilots, **weather forecasting**, testing the strength of a building design.

items.enonce_markdown: A driving school wants to use a driving simulator for new learners. State two advantages and two disadvantages of this choice.
items.solution_markdown:
Advantages (any two): learners can practise dangerous situations without risk; no fuel or vehicle damage so it is cheaper; the same situation can be repeated many times.

Disadvantages (any two): it does not feel exactly like a real road; buying and setting up the equipment is expensive; learners still need real driving practice.

items.enonce_markdown: A bakery model has these inputs: loaves per day 300, price 100 FCFA, ingredient cost 60 FCFA per loaf and daily rent 6,000 FCFA. Profit = loaves $\times$ (price $-$ cost) $-$ rent. Calculate (a) the profit, (b) the profit if the price is 120 FCFA and sales fall to 250 loaves, and (c) the least number of loaves that must be sold at 120 FCFA for the profit to be at least the profit in (a). Name the technique used.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $300 \times (100 - 60) - 6000 = 6,000$ FCFA.

(b) $250 \times (120 - 60) - 6000 = 9,000$ FCFA.

(c) Each loaf at 120 FCFA gives $120 - 60 = 60$ FCFA. We need $n \times 60 - 6000 \ge 6000$, so $n \times 60 \ge 12,000$, so $n \ge 200$. The least number is **200 loaves**.

The technique is **what-if analysis**, a simple simulation.

items_markdown: A model represents a real system; a simulation runs the model on a computer to imitate the system.
Advantages: safe, cheaper, saves time, repeatable and able to test what cannot be done in reality.
Disadvantages: results depend on the quality of the model and data, building it costs, and real tests are still needed.
Trying different values in a spreadsheet model to see results is what-if analysis.
In an exam answer, give the advantage or disadvantage, the reason and the situation.
